lead: The user interface is the part of the software a person actually touches: the screens, the buttons, the messages. Everything else — the database, the architecture, the patterns in 3.4 — stays hidden. So users judge quality by the interface alone. Interface design is the activity that decides what appears on each screen, in what order, and which control the user presses. It is used wherever a human sits at the end of the software: a UPI payment screen, an IRCTC ticket booking, a hospital reception counter, a shop's billing terminal.
prereq: You need: 3.1 (usability as a quality attribute) and Unit 2 (use cases supply the tasks the interface must support).

blocks.text: A user never sees your architecture. They see a screen, press a button, and decide whether the software is good. Usability — easy to learn, efficient to use, easy to remember — is a quality attribute, and the interface is where it is judged (see 3.1). Three rules cover most interface decisions.

items: Rule 1 — place the user in control. The user decides what happens next. Every long action has a Cancel, and nothing irreversible happens without a confirmation: show the bill, then take the money.

Rule 2 — reduce the user's memory load. The screen remembers, the user does not. Show a value the system already knows as read-only text instead of asking for it again, and offer a drop-down of valid choices instead of a blank box the user must fill from memory.

Rule 3 — make the interface consistent. The same thing looks and behaves the same everywhere. Use one word for one action on every screen — "Pay" everywhere, not "Pay" here and "Submit" there — and give each colour and icon one fixed meaning.

blocks.text: Each rule turns into concrete moves: a Cancel button, a read-only amount, a drop-down of states, one action word. Those moves are what earns marks. "Make it attractive and simple" is not an answer.
Four analyses come before any screen is drawn. Their input is the requirements model, above all the use cases of Unit 2.

items: User analysis — who uses it, and how skilled are they? A first-time customer, a clerk who uses it 200 times a day, a manager who opens it monthly. Experts want keyboard shortcuts; beginners want full labels.
Task analysis — what must the user do, in what order? Take each use case and list its steps: identify the account, see the amount, pay, get a receipt.
Content analysis — what is displayed on each screen: text, numbers, dates, photos, a chart? A 12-digit number needs spacing; a rupee amount needs two decimals.
Environment analysis — where is it used? A counter in bright sunlight, a crowded bus, a noisy shop floor, a quiet office. Light, screen size, network speed and interruptions all change the design.

blocks.text: Then comes the design step: choose the layout and the controls for each screen. Then evaluation: build a cheap prototype — paper or a clickable mock — put a real user in front of it, and count where they hesitate. Fix those places and evaluate again. The loop ends when the hesitation stops.

sections.h3: GUI elements and what each is for

blocks.text: A modern graphical interface is built from a small set of controls. Each has one job and one rule of use.

head: Element
What it is for
One rule
rows: Menu bar
Main command groups across the top of the window
Group by user task, not by program module
Pull-down menu
Items that open under a menu bar title
Keep it short; push rare commands deeper
Context menu
Right-click items for the object under the pointer
Only shortcuts to actions available elsewhere
Window
A resizable frame holding one task
One main window per task
Icon
A small picture standing for an action or a file
Pair it with a text label
Button
The control that triggers an action
One primary button per screen, visually strongest
Panel
A box that groups related fields
Group by meaning; keep each group small
Scroll bar
Shows position and moves through content longer than the window
Never hide an essential action below the fold
Error message
Text that explains a failure
Say what happened and what to do next

blocks.text: Layouts repeat so often that they are interface design patterns: list-and-detail, a wizard for a long form, a search bar at the top. Reuse a known pattern before inventing one, for the same reason you reuse the patterns of 3.4 — it is cheaper and users already know it.
An error message is the interface at its most stressful, so it needs the strictest rules.

items: Say what happened, in plain language: "The consumer number must be 12 digits", not "ERR-4071".
Say what to do next: "Check the number printed on your bill and type it again".
Put the message next to the field that caused it, keep everything the user already typed, and never let a bare code be the whole message.

blocks.text: Accessibility means the interface still works for people with low vision, colour blindness, or no mouse. Three basics: body text at least about 16 px on a phone, with a contrast ratio of at least 4.5:1 for normal text; never let colour alone carry a meaning, so an error is red and has an icon and words; and every control reachable by keyboard alone, with a visible focus outline. Usability and accessibility testing is covered in Unit 4.

figure.caption: Four analyses feed one interface design, and the prototype test loops back to refine it. Notice that evaluation is a step inside design, not something done after it.

spec.title: Interface design steps
spec.aria: Four analysis steps feed the interface design, which is then evaluated and sent back for refinement.

examples.question: An electricity-bill payment screen asks for (i) the consumer number, 12 digits, (ii) the amount, typed twice for confirmation, and (iii) a bill ID the user must copy from an SMS received that morning. (a) Count the memory items the user must hold in mind and name the golden rules that are broken. (b) Redesign it so the consumer number fetches the bill, the amount appears as read-only text, and the second amount entry is dropped. Count input boxes and memory items before and after.
steps: List what the user must recall. (i) The 12-digit consumer number. (ii) The amount, typed a second time to confirm it. (iii) The bill ID, copied from an SMS. Memory items before = 3.
Name the broken rules. "Reduce the user's memory load" is broken three times over. "Place the user in control" is also broken: the user cannot see the bill before paying, and cannot cancel.

Count input boxes before: consumer number, amount, amount again, bill ID = 4 boxes. (Some solutions count the doubled amount entry as one field and report 3 boxes; state your counting rule and you are safe either way.)

Redesign. The consumer number alone fetches the bill. The amount appears as read-only text, so there is no retyping and no second box. The bill ID disappears from the form because it arrives with the fetched bill.
Count input boxes after: consumer number only = 1 box. Boxes removed = 4 − 1 = 3.
Count memory items after: only the consumer number is recalled = 1 item. Memory items removed = 3 − 1 = 2.
examples.answer: Memory items fall from 3 to 1 and input boxes from 4 to 1, so 3 boxes are removed and 2 remembered items are removed.
examples.check:
memory_before = 3   # 12-digit consumer number, amount retyped, bill ID from SMS
fields_before = 4   # consumer number, amount, amount again, bill ID
fields_after = 1    # consumer number only; amount becomes read-only text
memory_after = 1    # only the consumer number is recalled
fields_removed = fields_before - fields_after
print(memory_before)
print(fields_before)
print(fields_after)
print(fields_removed)
print(memory_after)

traps: "Make it attractive and simple" scores nothing. Marks come from naming the analysis step, the golden rule, and one concrete control.
Do not count each field as one memory item. Count each distinct thing the user must recall — a number, an amount, a code read from an SMS.
Interface design is not GUI coding and not architectural design; it starts after the task and content are analysed.
A bare code as an error message ("Error 4071") is always wrong. Say what happened and what to do next.
Skipping environment analysis is a favourite slip: a screen that works in a quiet office fails at a counter in bright sunlight.

quiz.q: State the three golden rules of user interface design.
quiz.a: Place the user in control; reduce the user's memory load; make the interface consistent.

quiz.q: Name the four analyses done before the interface is designed.
quiz.a: User analysis, task analysis, content analysis, environment analysis.

quiz.q: Why does a read-only amount display reduce memory load more than a pre-filled editable box?
quiz.a: The user neither retypes nor re-checks the value, and the box cannot be edited by mistake; the screen holds the value and the user only reads it.

quiz.q: Give the three rules for writing an error message.
quiz.a: Plain language saying what happened; a line saying what to do next; placed next to the field, keeping the user's input, with no bare code.

quiz.q: A form asks for the date of birth in a free text box as DD/MM/YYYY, and half the users type MM/DD/YYYY. Which analysis step tells you the format matters, and what control change fixes it?
quiz.a: Content analysis: the item is a date, not free text. Replace the box with a date picker, or three drop-downs for day, month and year.

quiz.q: A payment screen asks for an account number (10 digits), a PIN (4 digits remembered separately), and an OTP read from an SMS. Count the memory items and state one redesign move.
quiz.a: Three memory items: account number, PIN, OTP. Redesign move: let a saved payee or a contact picker fill the account number, so only two items remain.

quiz.q: A screen shows eight buttons of the same colour and size, and the same save action is labelled "Save" on one screen and "Update" on another. Which golden rule is broken, and what are two fixes?
quiz.a: Consistency is broken twice: visual weight and word choice. Fix by making one primary button visually strongest and using one word, "Save", on every screen.

beyond: Not for the exam. In industry, interface design has largely moved to design systems: a shared library of colours, spacing and components that every team reuses, so consistency stops depending on individual discipline. Usability heuristics from Jakob Nielsen and the WCAG accessibility guidelines are the common checklist sources you will meet on the job. Modern practice also tests with small numbers of real users early rather than sign-off meetings late. Search next for "design system", "usability heuristics" and "WCAG contrast ratio" if you want the working detail.
